In focusing his singular sense of humor on the science fiction film genre, Mel Brooks realized the ease with which he could have milked a few extra laughs by employing deliberately poor special effects. But instead, he wanted his parody to work within the context of a high-gloss production. To this end, he enlisted visual effects supervisor Peter Donen. Working primarily with Apogee - but with outside input from Illusion Arts and Industrial Light and Magic - Donen was able to orchestrate a full and varied array of cinematic illusions. Article by Mark Elliot. 26 Witch Trials For director George Miller, The Witches of Eastwick was a formidable challenge - a supernatural comedy with a top-notch cast that required a deft touch to maintain its proper balance of humor and horror. Though effects would take a back seat in the production, it was necessary that they be brought to bear on such thorny problems as depicting a palatial mansion that did not exist, creating a tennis ball with a mind of its own and transforming actor Jack Nicholson into a fifty-foot demon. Engaged to accomplish these and other feats were Industrial Light and Magic and makeup effects artist Rob Bottin. Article by Adam Eisenberg. 46 Masters of the Universe Though derived from a phenomenally popular toy line, Masters of the Universe would prove to be anything but fun and games for production designer William Stout, visual effects supervisor Richard Edlund and makeup artist Michael Westmore. With high expectations but minimal time and resources, the design and effects teams had to translate plastic dolls into flesh-and-blood characters, create a faraway fantasy world from scratch and implant nonstop optical trickery into a sword-andsorcery adventure of extravagant proportions. In the intervening years, film audiences were shown the mystery, horror and wonder of alien worlds and creatures - sometimes even the humor - but a parodic perspective was rarely taken. Parody, however, has been the cornerstone of Mel Brooks' career. As a director, his first cinematic spoof, The Producers, took aim at Broadway musicals. Rewarded with a cult following, Brooks next lampooned westerns, horror films, suspense thrillers and even the history of man with his comic send-ups Blazing Saddles, Young Frankenstein, High Anxiety and History of the World - Part I. Given Brooks' past, it was inevitable that he would one day skewer the future - and so he has with Spaceballs, his $22 million backhanded salute to science fiction films past and present. Spaceballs begins - as did Star Wars, its.principal target - with an immense space cruiser rumbling past the camera. Commanded by the evil Dark Helmet - Rick Moranis as a stunted Darth Vader type - and his cowardly cohort, Colonel Sandurz, Spaceball One is en route to the peaceful planet of Druidia to steal its atmosphere. Under the leadership of President Skroob - played by Mel Brooks - the sinister Spaceballs have foolishly expended their own planet's atmospheric resources. The crafty Druidians, however, have made access difficult by erecting a transparent air shield around their entire planet. To gain entrance, the Spaceballs intend to abduct the Druish Princess Vespa - bethrothed in marriage to sleepy Prince Valium - and then ransom her for the combination to the air shield door. Leaving her boring prince at the altar, Vespa flees the wedding ceremony in her spaceborne Mercedes honeymoon coupe - accompanied by her droid of honor, Dot Matrix - but then is drawn into the awaiting Spaceball cruiser. Alerted to the princess' plight, King Roland of Druidia desperately seeks help from hero-for-hire Lone Starr and his sidekick Barf. And thus begins Chapter 11 of the Spaceballs saga. With only one year from project approval to release - a tough schedule for a major effects film - Mel Brooks promptly engaged the capable, efficiency-conscious Peter Donen to oversee the production of Spaceballs' visual effects. Prior to Spaceballs, Donen had been postproduction supervisor and laboratory liaison for Kaleidoscope Film Effects, and had then served as vice-president and director at Cinema Research. After eight years at Cinema Research, Donen satisfied a long-time personal goal and became a freelance effects supervisor on Flight of the Navigator. Though Brooks himself oversaw much of the effects work on Spaceballs, Donen felt that as visual effects supervisor he was given an ample free hand. "Mel is a wonderful director to work for. He is overflowing with enthusiasm and he keeps everybody at that level. He is intimately involved in the creative aspects of everything that is done, yet he has the ultimate faith in his department heads to hire them and just let them get on 145

with their work." Even as Brooks made his last major changes to the script in March 1986, Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer - the project's principal backer - was scheduling Spaceballs for a summer release the following year. "Getting an advance start was a necessity," observed Donen. "The movie was to be in theaters before the first of July, which for an effects picture of this type was a remarkably short period of time - especially when you consider that this picture is a comedy, and comedies require extensive previewing. Mel was faced with a dilemma. Should he let the effects people go immediately, making what changes he could later, or should he have them start after the picture had finished shooting and not make it for summer? The decision was to go for summer and let everyone contribute as much as possible. Consequently, once we had storyboards on seventy or eighty percent of the pure effects shots, we put Spaceballs into production. We were allowed to start building and shooting before principal was even in testing. This was great for our people since it allowed us the luxury to control the budget and the schedule. As a result, we were able to prepare this picture as efficiently as any effects picture has been prepared." After Brooks' selection of Peter Donen, a decision was needed as to the company or companies that would actually do the work. "The movie is about mayhem and madness in space," Donen noted, "but at the same time we went for a realistic effect. We did not show wires and blue lines intentionally. The jokes are not in the effects. Instead, the jokes are in the story and the events that occur." Since Spaceballs is a parody of many high-quality effects pictures, its effects had to be of the same caliber. For the bulk of the work, M-G-M first approached Industrial Light and Magic, hoping the Lucasfilm organization would enjoy the opportunity to poke some good-natured fun at its Star Wars saga. Too busy with other assignments to accept the project in full, ILM nevertheless agreed to provide Spaceballs with one short sequence involving a puppetized alien. M-G-M's subsequent selection of Apogee as the prime effects contractor resulted in a unique reunion. At the completion of Star Wars - nearly ten years before - the high-powered effects team that had been formed specifically for that project divided in two. Part of the unit, led by Richard Edlund and Dennis Muren, moved north to the Lucasfilm complex in Marin County, taking with them the proprietary corporate name. The remaining crew members, headed by John Dykstra, stayed behind in the original Van Nuys facility and rechristened themselves Apogee, Inc. Spaceballs marked the first time since Star Wars that the two units had labored together on a single project. Apogee's success as a special effects house is due in part to its diversified staff. Jonathan Erland is head of research and development at the facility - a position unique in the visual effects industry. In 1984, he distinguished himself and his company with an Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences scientific and engineering award for codeveloping - with optical supervisor Roger Dorney - the reverse bluescreen traveling matte process first used in Firefox, The following year he shared two additional awards for technical achievement - one for the high-power 'Blue Max' front projector developed for 2010, and another for improved design and construction of front projection screens. Before Spaceballs went into production, Erland participated in a successful industry-wide effort to produce a new motion picture film stock optimized for visual effects. "The principal effects houses such as Apogee, ILM and Boss worked closely with Kodak in developing the film," Erland explained. "Kodak built the film specifically for our bluescreen traveling matte technology because the effects community expressed concern about the effectiveness of their 5294 film stock for generating mattes. It's a wonderfully fast film for ordinary photography, but 5294 is essentially useless for traveling matte photography. The problem is that fast film is grainier than slower film, and a fast film has more trouble recording pure blue light without also exposing the red and particularly the green layers of the emulsion. Both of these properties make the film exceedingly difficult to use in visual effects. So we brought our troubles to the attention of Kodak. They conducted a series of seminars with the effects community which covered many issues, including film stock. This precipitated much interest from Kodak, leading to the research and development of 5295, a film that retained the same speed as 5294 while exhibiting the matting properties of the older, slower film. Beyond that, they incorporated new tolerances on film perforation, which for our kind of work was extremely important. If perforations are cut inconsistently, then even the steadiest camera movement will not insure a rock-solid image. Kodak cut the error tolerances for the perforations in half, resulting in a much steadier film that helps keep our images from floating around." While Star Trek /V used the new 5295 film stock for one scene, Spaceballs is the first motion picture to employ it throughout for all of its live-action bluescreen work. In the film's opening scene, Spaceball One enters frame and glides ominously past the camera - seemingly forever - in an outlandish parody of the breathtaking lead-in to Star Wars. Due to the size and complexity of the model required, Mel Brooks commissioned the Apogee model shop - headed by Star Wars Oscar winner Grant McCune - to begin construction on the ship even before a determination was made that Apogee would be Spaceballs' overall effects contractor. McCune was assisted in the task by model shop designer Chris Ross, effects art director Stephen Dane and a shipload of talented modelmakers. "Initially," stated Ross, "Terence Marsh - the production designer for Spaceballs - sent us a relatively small conceptual drawing for the cruiser. We were further instructed by Brooks to build a cruiser 'so big that a person would get jet-lag by going from one end to the other.' From Marsh's drawing, I created the top view of the cruiser in two-and-a-half weeks, breaking it down methodically into sections because the fullsize drawing was huge - seventeen-feet, four-inches long. After the drawings were completed, we shipped them over to Marsh who accepted ninety-nine percent of what we did." Dane, meanwhile, was already developing a construction approach. "Chris did the design a section at a time. Then I translated his flat drawings into three-dimensional form so the sections would stack well. I had to determine the size of the shaft that they would be mounted on, clearance for the neon tubes and space for motion control motors. The inside of the model was like a densely packed engine compartment in a Japanese car. Building the cruiser was like making a Liberty ship in the Second World War. We fabricated the sections assembly-line style and staked them on the main supporting tube like meat and bell peppers on a shish kebab. The inspiration for the detail on the Spaceball cruiser came from a fourfoot model of the Japanese battleship Yamato. We studied this ship because it was the most heavily armed ship ever built. Some of the little gun turrets became incorporated into our design. In fact, the battleship model itself eventually disappeared onto the Spaceball cruiser. It made wonderful texture." "Because the surface area of the ship was so massive," noted Ross, "we had to modulate all of the skin to give it scale. We made a basic mold for the skin from our extensive ten-year-old graveyard of model kits. The basic pattern for the mold was fourteen-by-fourteen inches; and it was very modular in its design, allowing it to be cut up in a variety of ways. The cut pieces were glued onto the surface of the model in different combinations and orientations. The ship would have been extremely heavy if we had used regular building materials, so we decided to cast the detailed sections in very light microballoonfilled urethane. While the model was planned in much detail, it's impossible to design every square inch of it; and so the final detailing was left to our team of model builders." Construction completed, the cruiser was rolled from the model shop to the production stage where it was photographed over a period of weeks by effects cameramen David Hardberger and John Sullivan, with assistants Stephen Brooks and Mark Gredell. Though certainly the largest, the Spaceball cruiser was not the only miniature craft constructed for the film. The Eagle 5 - a battered Winnebago camper with delta wings and rocket engines grafted onto it - is the cramped and cluttered home of heroes Lone Starr and Barf. "The Eagle 5 was the most difficult model to do," observed McCune, "because it was an exact, onetwelfth-scale miniature copy of a real vehicle - which was unusual for us since seventy to eighty percent of models we do are futuristic designs and have no real counterparts. When doing something this small and intricate, there cannot be eight people working on it. Instead, it's best to have a few people working for a longer time. For this reason, I gave the Eagle 5 to just two people - Cory Faucher and Smokey Stover. Between them, they had eight weeks to complete the model." The initial shot of the Eagle 5 begins with the camera facing the front of the vehicle. Then the view sweeps to the side where 'Eagle 5' can be seen emblazoned on the door. Below the lettering is an insignia depicting a screaming eagle with dollar bills clutched in each claw and an inscription that reads 'Captain Lone Starr - Hero for Hire.' Finally, the Eagle 5 passes by, revealing an 'I Love Uranus' bumper sticker. Motion control camera work for the shot was performed by head camera operator Doug Smith, assisted by Glenn Campbell and Ron Robinson. "The Eagle 5 shot was fairly complicated," Smith commented. "It's tough to film a model anytime the camera travels 180 degrees around it, but the hardest part was getting feedback from Mel for the timing of the sequence. It was very important to get the right pacing for the jokes on the door and the bumper. Because of that, the shot was done several times." Clint Colver and his animation department were responsible for the starfield that had to move in swirling consonance with the ship. "The camera rotates around the Eagle 5 and focuses on several details while the starfield behind it swings around 180 degrees," Colver explained. "The background was challenging to animate because the stars had to move in the opposite direction of the vehicle so that the ship would appear to be moving forward. John Shourt plotted the position of the starfield at different points in the shot. Then the computer in our motion controlled animation stand determined a smooth path through these points. From there we continued making refinements to the move until it looked perfect." On board the Eagle 5, Lone Starr is napping at the controls while Barf is snacking on dog biscuits. Barf is, after all, a Mawg - half-man, half-dog and his own best friend. Makeup artist Ken Diaz worked with makeup supervisor Ben Nye, Jr. in developing the offbeat character. "Barf's makeup went through many changes," Diaz recalled. "Originally we sculpted a full-face mask resembling a bulldog with many wrinkles. However, Mel Brooks discarded it because he wanted audiences to be able to recognize John Candy who was playing the part. So I sculpted a nose and upper lip piece that Candy liked - but again Brooks felt it covered too much. In fact, he joked that if we were going to hide Candy behind a mask, he might as well hire someone else for half the price. Finally we settled on a fur patch over one eye and a rubber-gum application applied to the end of John Candy's nose. The top of his head was built up a bit and ears were constructed from foam rubber with fur attached, then laid over the actuating mechanics that moved them. Finally, a fur hair net slid over the ears and covered the rest of the headpiece." Peter Albiez and his group were called upon to provide the articulation for Barf's floppy ears and wagging tail. The tail - developed by Ray Robinson - was fairly straightforward and easy to activate. John Candy, in fact, was able to trigger it himself by means of a switch hidden within his jumpsuit. The ears, however, were more complex. Animatronics designer Rick Lazzarini used his Macintosh computer extensively in devising the required mechanisms. "Using a digitizer, I traced over a photo of John Candy in order to create a picture of him with

the dog ears attached. I then transported the ears as a separate graphic into MacDraft - sort of a poor man's CAD (computer aided design) system - to produce a mechanical drawing of the sophisticated understructure that would make the ears move. Pivot points, core shapes and cable attachments were plotted out on screen. Upon printout, these drawings were affixed to delrin plastic, which was then scribed and machined accordingly. These resulting plastic pieces acted as lightweight joints in the internal structure. Six axes of movement were incorporated into each ear, giving them the ability to move much like a human hand. The ears were affixed to a lightweight fiberglass skullcap, with cables running under a wig and down the back. Using MacDraft, I was able to preview the most efficient layout of the necessary radio control servos, cable routes, batteries and receivers, which were then assembled and attached to a back harness and hidden under Candy's costume. In addition to designing and creating the ears, I also operated them on the set - with Ray Robinson assisting. It was truly an acting job, trying to react to the dialogue along with Candy, anticipating his expressions and making his ears 'emote' appropriately." Although three separate versions of the ears had been requested and produced - cable-controlled, radio-controlled and self-controlled - the radio-controlled pair was used exclusively during the shoot because of its simplicity of operation. SEESE Leisure activities aboard the Eagle 5 are interrupted by a threatening transmission from Pizza the Hutt. Similar in basic shape and demeanor to Star Wars' Jabba the Hutt, space gangster Pizza the Hutt is a bubbling mountain of pepperoni and he character was cheese. Designed by Screaming Mad George, the character was sculpted in clay and then cast in foam by the makeup unit. Mechanics were provided by the physical effects crew. Though Pizza's voice was provided by Dom DeLuise, it was actor Richard Karron who had the dubious honor of donning the suit. "We controlled the large articulated mouth with cables," said Peter Albiez, "and the bubbling came from air bladders inflating and deflating inside the costume. Through tubes we piped out smoke and melting cheese - which actually was pancake flour mixed with water and yellow coloring, We also smeared pepperoni over his face - and in the take that was used, a slice of it slides off and into his mouth. It was pretty funny." The approved take would not be captured on the first try, however. Brooks' reaction to the initial mouth articulations was negative, and so the mechanics were modified and the figure reshot a few weeks later - with Rick Lazzarini inside. "Of all the suits I've been in," said Lazzarini, "of all the puppeteering I've done from cramped quarters, this was by far the grungiest. Luckily, it worked out well." Peter Albiez and his unit were also called upon to construct Dot Matrix - dubbed 'She-3PO' by the film crew. "Donfeld - who was costume designer for the film - came up with the concept for Dot Matrix," noted Albiez. "She had golden armor, metallic hair and a swiveling head - and her face looked somewhat like Joan Rivers' who was going to be providing the voice. Once Mel Brooks approved the design, we made a full-body mold of Lorene Yarnell who would actually be playing the character - pulling a standard lifecast of her head and then wrapping her body with plaster-soaked bandages. From these molds, a full-size plaster casting was made and then covered with about an inch of clay that we carved into the proper shape for Dot. Since the outer surface of the clay would be the inner surface of the suit, the one-inch thickness gave Yarnell plenty of room inside. In the head, we allowed extra room for the infrared lights in Dot's eyes and the radio control mechanisms that dilated her pupils. We also allowed additional room in the chest area for an alarm and flashing display. Another mold was made from the clay sculpture - and from that a strong fiberglass statue was formed. Styrene plastic was vacuformed over the fiberglass, then removed and vacuum-metallized with brass to give Dot her shiny gold appearance. For the interior scenes, her feet were outfitted with roller skates; but for the desert exteriors, she was given flat-bottomed shoes. Enough parts were created for six complete Dot Matrix costumes - which was fortunate, since we needed them all due to breakage." To camouflage joins and gaps in the costume, the wardrobe department made a gold spandex body suit for Yarnell - half of the renowned Shields and Yarnell mime team - fitting it with tabs so the plastic android shell could be mounted onto her like a suit of armor. "At first it took forty minutes to suit her up," Albiez recalled, "but eventually we got it down to twenty minutes. Since there was little in the way of natural ventilation, Lorene was kept cool between scenes by running air hoses into the head and body of the suit. Also, it was easy for her to take a breather between takes since the helmet was built to pop off quickly. Even though we were shooting in October, it was important to keep her cool - especially during the desert scenes near Yuma where the temperature was ninetyfive degrees. It was difficult for her to walk - especially through the dunes - because her eyes were hidden behind a perforated metal plate that offered only a six-degree field of view. Despite her discomforts, Lorene played a very funny C-3PO." As with other expansive scenes in the film, Spaceball City was rendered in the form of an elaborate matte painting. Selected to produce the paintings for Spaceballs was Illusion Arts, a relatively new company headed by some veteran talents in the field - Bill Taylor and Syd Dutton. After having his head rematerialized on backwards by the malfunctioning transporter, Skroob shuns the device and simply walks next door to the control center. "To simulate the swirling energy surrounding Skroob in the transporter," recalled Clint Colver, "we used a moire pattern. Essentially, a moire results when one piece of negative film scribed with fine lines is moved over another similarly scribed piece of film to produce a scintillating effect. A surprising range of textures can be achieved by varying the pattern, size, shape and speed of the artwork." In their takeover attempt, the Spaceballs fire laser blasts around the royal Mercedes and then lock onto it with a powerful tractor beam. "In the scene where the cruiser attacks Vespa's honeymoon coupe," explained Colver, "there were several animated laser shots that exploded like flak bursts. To get that effect, we filmed explosions on one of our stages and then mounted that footage frame by frame onto animation cels which were then aligned and rephotographed on our animation stand. In the process, the explosions drift backwards through the frame so the ship - photographed by Mat Beck - would appear to be moving forward. The tractor beam was trickier and had more texture than the laser blasts. To simulate this beam, we used a diffused moire interference pattern to add textural interest." On the starcruiser bridge, Dark Helmet and Sandurz watch through giant windows as the princess' ship is drawn toward their vessel. "The bridge of the Spaceball cruiser required an enormous blue screen," Jon Erland noted. "At first we considered using a backlit blue transmission screen - which invariably produces the best results - but the screen needed to be thirty feet tall by one-hundred-and-twenty feet long and it just was not practical to build a seamless transmission screen that large. Our solution to this problem would normally have been to use our 'Blue Max' blue flux front projector. The 'Blue Max' is capable of projecting blue light onto an extremely large Scotchlite retro-reflective screen and was used to produce the monumental bluescreen sequences in 2010 and Dune. However, because we wanted to emphasize the enormity of the bridge set, it was necessary to use a very wide-angle lens - and such a lens would overshoot our beamsplitter. We did use the 'Blue Max' for the scene when Barf climbs a ladder between the Eagle 5 and the honeymoon coupe, but for the bridge set we were forced to fall back on the most basic and least desirable method of all - frontlit bluebacking. Historically, a pure clean blue light has not been obtainable from a frontlit backing because the backing itself is either painted blue or made of blue fabric that reflects a very broad band of blue. Since the only way to get pure light off of them is to put pure light onto them, backings of this kind are normally lit by incandescent lights with blue filters attached. However, since only a very small portion of the light from an incandescent lamp is blue, a tremendous number of lamps would be required to illuminate a screen as wide as the one needed for Spaceballs - not to mention the fact that the blue gelatin filters on the lights would constantly be burning out and need replenishing." After considering a variety of mercury vapor lamps - which are more efficient at producing blue light - Erland and his associates eventually opted to design their own high-output fluorescent tube incorporating an internal reflector with a specially selected phosphor compatible with the new 5295 film stock. "Coupled with this," Erland continued, "we wanted a way to power the fluorescent tubes that would not cause problems of its own. Most fluorescent lights employ a conventional ballast - which is a big noisy thing used to transform power to drive the tube. Since we needed approximately one thousand tubes to illuminate this enormous backing, we expected a chorus of noise from all these ballasts. Moreover, the ballasts operate at 120 cycles, so high-speed photography would run into strobing problems. We overcame these difficulties by using a highfrequency solid state power supply that effectively eliminated both the strobing and the noise. In the end, we were able to assemble these one thousand tubes with their power supplies on the Spaceballs set in the nick of time - just two days before the shoot, in fact. Though an obvious choice, it was soon discovered that real jam was not up to the task. "Real raspberry jam was thick like putty," said Chris Ross, "and what we wanted was something that really flowed. So I thinned it with Super Goop, a clear syrupy substance. I also used a white opaque fluid to make the

jam more readable on camera. The real jam was too dark, almost dropping off to black. The structure itself was a steel boiler end plate - two-and-a-half feet in diameter and a quarter-inch thick - detailed to look like a radar dish. It was a mess when it hit the radar dish - jam went everywhere - and Grant and I had the job of cleaning up after every take. And on that very night, as if in response to their unwitting conjury, a mysterious stranger comes to town - a man of wit and charm with money to burn and a prodigious sexual appetite. He studied that for about a week and then just went ahead and drew one - totally free-hand. It looked so fluid and whiplike that there was really no point in trying for anything better. He did three whip shots in all - spending about two weeks on each one. Later, when we tried compositing them with the plates, we realized that the whip needed a core of some kind because the effect looked a little flat - so Mauro went back in and added a core to the original animation. The outer section and the core were shot as separate high-contrast elements, then colored and diffused in optical." The unexpected arrival of He-Man's friends and allies turns the tide. Freed from his bonds, He-Man confronts Skeletor for the last time as the two sworn enemies square off in a swordswinging, bone-crunching battle to the bitter end - but there was no end, bitter or otherwise. "The big climax, where He-Man does Skeletor in was just not there," Windell reported. "We had always planned on sending Skeletor over the altar and through the big window behind it - but that was never shot, and now the Castle Greyskull set no longer existed except in pieces. Gary asked us to come up with something that would make the sequence work. We had to kill off Skeletor in a dramatic way, using the material they'd already shot as a basis - and whatever we decided to do had to be completed in one day. In other words, there couldn't be more than about a dozen shots. Gary had mentioned at one time that he wanted to have a soldier thrown into the bottomless pit of Castle Greyskull to show the depth of it. So Richard, Bill Neil and I finally decided to send Skeletor into the pit - which Gary thought was a great idea. Now all we had to do was figure out how to do that dramatically and quickly. There was already a pretty substantial amount of battle footage between He-Man and Skeletor, but they were missing the crucial story point. So I went over all the footage with the film's editor, Anne V. Coates, and our effects editor, Dennis Michaelson, sketched out where the sequence ended and where we had to end up, and came up with a series of shots that would hopefully bridge the gap. "There were a number of minor story points we had to take into account to successfully complete the sequence, some of which helped us and some of which hurt. Just prior to the beginning of the fight, we see Skeletor's costume change from black to gold - which was a problem since the only element we had shot bluescreen of Skeletor falling through space showed him in his ordinary black costume. Therefore I had to get Skeletor's costume to change from gold to black sometime during the fight sequence. As it turned out, I did it in the first

shot we picked up, where He-Man seizes Skeletor's staff. My first insert showed He-Man breaking the staff. There's a huge explosion, and we see Skeletor's costume metamorphosing. So that was fairly easily handled." Of greater potential consequence was the fact that the throneroom battle site had already been disassembled - and obviously could not be resurrected intact. "Without realizing it, Gary had decided to do something early in the sequence that allowed us to finish the fight. When the two swords first clash, there was a big blast of energy and the entire Greyskull throneroom receded into darkness, leaving Skeletor and He-Man fighting in a smoky, darkly-lit set. We had only a black stage on which to shoot, but fortunately some of the set pieces had been kept. Thanks to that, Bill Neil was able to create a lighting scheme that we could match to the original footage. We realized that if we were going to throw Skeletor into the pit we needed to stage our fight right at the edge. Consequently, we built the edge of the pit on a rostrum so we could shoot up from inside it and down into it. We also had another insert area for the throne, with smoke and light around it. The only problem we had now was to get out of that dark environment to the normal lighting scheme at the end where He-Man is standing victoriously in front of the throne. I went through all the material that had been shot on the original throneroom set and found about half a dozen background shots, out of which there were four we could actually use as the transition from dark to light. Once I found the background I needed to make it work, I knew we could shoot He-Man against a blue screen and matte him into it." "It was a real simple solution," Bill Neil commented, "a quick way of tying directly into all the existing footage and making it work. Terry's fight sequence picked up on the last gesture we were cutting on and lead right into the new material as though that's how it had been planned all along. The greatest challenge for me was to create the illusion that the set was still there, just from a few strategically placed components, and to match the live-action cinematographer's lighting style. This was months later, so when I talked to the cameraman and his gaffer on the telephone, neither of them could remember exactly what they had done at the time. It had all been done at the spur of the moment on the last night of the shoot - and they hadn't wrapped until two o'clock in the morning! All things considered, I think it matches pretty well." In addition to shooting the handful of scenes required to complete the preempted fight, Neil also photographed plates for two last-minute matte paintings. "Both shots were afterthoughts," said Matthew Yuricich. "The first one showed only a portion of the pit as Skeletor and He-Man wrestle shoulder-to-shoulder at the edge - that one was painted by Michele Moen. The other painting showed the full pit from directly overhead, looking straight down into the middle of it as Skeletor falls through." With the live-action finally completed and in the can, Neil was able to turn his attention to the remaining postproduction effects shots. Included were motion control scenes of Skeletor's miniature battlestation that had to fit perfectly into live-action background plates. Perspective and alignment considerations were particularly critical when the battlestation was supposed to be cruising the streets of Whittier at night. "This was very different from most of the space-type shots we handle," Neil commented. "Here we were in a completely realistic environment, so we had to fit our miniature elements perfectly into the perspective of the scene. If it had been shot in space, the accuracy of the ship's trajectory would have been far less critical. Here, however, we had a great deal more information in the frame and the ship had to fit precisely into all of it. It had to grow in size as it approached the camera and it had to lay right into the existing perspective lines. Then, as the battlestation passed down the tree-lined street - backlit by moonlight - we had to add shadows that would be cast onto the ship by the trees. The timing of these elements and their exact trajectories also became a problem, because any discrepancy at all would be picked up immediately - even by an untrained eye - and would instantly reveal the presence of a foreign element in the shot. The moonlight in our live-action plate was actually cast by a Musco light placed a couple of blocks away from where we were shooting. These high-intensity lighting units come mounted on cranes, and in this case were employed to cast a three-quarter backlight across the scene. To help tie in the bluescreen miniature, I made up a long board with irregular Died it and shapes cut out of it. Then I motion-controlled it and dragged it through my key light - along with the battlestation - to make it appear as though a beam of moonlight were breaking through the trees and wiping light and shadow across the ship. There was one shot that was even more complex because it involved the battlestation floating down the street toward camera surrounded by live-action troops. In this case, the ship had to be paced to the walking troops while the shadows had to be paced to the speed the ship was moving past the trees." Neil's headaches in getting the pace of one element to match with that of another might almost serve as a true-life metaphor for Masters of the Universe - a film that came dangerously close to remaining unfinished and which suffered for its lack of preparation every step of the way. Either the pace was breakneck or painfully slow, especially in the case of Boss Film's crew who found the expression 'hurry up and wait' all too fitting, "A lot of people put a lot of blood into this project," Richard Edlund sighed, "both here and elsewhere. At Boss we were wounded by the hideous production problems - and it's a testament to our group that we were able to handle it all. Here we learned a basic 'koan' of life - 'koan' being a Zen term referring to a situation in which someone is presented with a puzzle and must come up with an answer. It doesn't matter whether the answer actually makes sense or not, so long as it solves the puzzle. The koan of life I'm talking about is that whenever we're faced with adversity, it's necessary to take that adversity and turn it to our advantage. We grew a lot as a result of our experience on Masters of the Universe."
